paras: The attempted lynching of Isom Strong took place at Henderson, Texas, on August 7, 1903, when a mob took Strong, a young Black prisoner, from a sheriff who had moved him out of town and prepared to lynch him. The mob gave him up after District Judge Levy promised that the grand jury would take up his case at once, and the next day Strong pleaded guilty and was sentenced to ninety-nine years in the penitentiary. White newspapers across the country carried the story as an example of a mob yielding to the law and of swift justice.

According to a special dispatch to the Dallas News from Henderson, Strong attempted on the night of August 6 to enter the bedroom of Mrs. Mollie Lacy, a widow. Mrs. Lacy woke and gave the alarm, and Strong was captured, identified by her and taken to jail. The dispatches described him only as "a young negro" and gave no account from him.

On the afternoon of August 7 the sheriff "quietly slipped" Strong out of town, but a mob followed, took the prisoner from the officers and brought him back to Henderson. Preparations were made to lynch him there. District Judge Levy then promised the mob that the grand jury would consider the case at once, and the mob dispersed and Strong was returned to jail. A follow-up dispatch from Henderson said the mob had held him "for the purpose of lynching him" and surrendered him that night.

On August 8 the grand jury indicted Strong for attempted criminal assault, and he was placed on trial the same day. He pleaded guilty, the jury fixed the penalty at ninety-nine years, and after he waived time he was sentenced and taken to the penitentiary that afternoon. The Bryan Morning Eagle, a Texas paper, gave the charge as "burglary and an attempt to commit criminal assault."

Shortly after Strong's conviction, another Black man, Emanuel Thompson, was brought in from Mount Enterprise, accused of attempting to assault a Miss Sparks, and was indicted, tried and given ninety-nine years the same afternoon. No report names any member of the mob or describes an arrest or prosecution of its members.

The mob story spread on August 8 through the Dallas News special and the wires, appearing that day in papers from Montgomery and Birmingham to Wichita, Cheyenne, Omaha, Indianapolis, Phoenix and Salt Lake City. Headlines cast the mob as law-abiding: the Wyoming Tribune ran "Texas Citizens Show Respect for the Law," the Indianapolis Journal "Mob Yields to Reason," and the Arizona Republican "All the Mob Wanted / Was That the Case Should Be Heard Speedily." The Montgomery Advertiser called it a "unique case," and weeklies in Kansas, South Dakota, Indiana and Mississippi reprinted the account through August 14 under headings such as "Judge Saved a Negro" and "The Mob Satisfied."

The Salt Lake Herald drew an editorial lesson, writing that Texas had furnished Indiana, Illinois and Delaware "with an example of law-enforcement." The sentencing wire of August 8 was headlined "Texas Court Does Some Rapid Work" in Birmingham, "Swift Justice Meted Out to the Texas Negro" in Wichita and "Two Negro Brutes Given Long Terms" in Savannah. The Sumter Watchman and Southron ran it on August 12 as "Better Than Lynching," and the Courier-Journal called Strong "a Bad Negro."
None of the reports gave Strong's own account or questioned the speed of a plea and sentence entered the day after a mob had held him. No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

Reports spelled the accused man's name as Isom Strong, Isham Strong, "L. Strong" and "Wilson Strang," and the widow's as Mollie Lacy, Millie Lacey and Milie Lacy. While the news dispatches said the mob took Strong from officers outside town, the Salt Lake Herald wrote that it took him "out of jail." Most copies of the sentencing wire gave the term as ninety-nine years, but the Wichita Daily Eagle printed ninety years.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Isom Strong
bases: A mob took a Black prisoner from the officers and made preparations to lynch him, then gave him up on a judge's promise of immediate grand jury action (A3, A1, A2); the later wire says he was taken 'for the purpose of lynching him' (A10).

A 'mob' with no lawful authority seized Strong from the officers over an accusation of entering a widow's bedroom and prepared to lynch him (A3, A2), but it dispersed and he was returned to jail alive, later sentenced to prison (A1, A10); this was an attempted lynching, not a killing.

The mob episode rests on a single Henderson dispatch (credited to a Dallas News special, A3) carried in many papers (A1, A2), but a separate Aug. 8 Henderson dispatch on the indictment and sentencing independently refers to the mob that had taken him 'for the purpose of lynching him' (A10), and a Texas paper confirms the sentence (A22).

accounts.label: Bryan Morning Eagle (Texas)
accounts.gist: Strong was sentenced to 99 years for 'burglary and an attempt to commit criminal assault'; the grand jury and trial court acted within about two hours.

accounts.label: Salt Lake Herald editorial
accounts.gist: A mob 'took a negro out of jail with intent to lynch him' but returned him after a judge's assurance of a speedy trial, an example to Indiana, Illinois and Delaware.

framing.detail: First-day headlines praised the outcome as lawful restraint: 'TEXAS CITIZENS SHOW RESPECT FOR THE LAW', 'MOB YIELDS TO REASON', 'ALL THE MOB WANTED / Was That the Case Should Be Heard Speedily', while recounting the mob's seizure and preparations to lynch.
The Salt Lake Herald offered Texas as 'an example of law-enforcement' to Northern states.
Sentencing headlines stressed speed and severity: 'TEXAS COURT DOES SOME RAPID WORK', 'Swift Justice Meted Out', 'Better Than Lynching', 'TWO NEGRO BRUTES GIVEN LONG TERMS'.
